subject: Why do I need a parameter for the hypermean...

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Why do I need a parameter for the hypermean...
parts:
Given some subject specific parameters theta_i ~ N(mu,sd)
If I assume a uniform hyperprior for mu, is there any need to assign it as a parameter to sample?
Or can I just as well treat theta_i ~ N(mean(theta),sd)

The latter approach seems to be working more efficiently for me than either a centered or non-centered parameterization of theta_i, and I haven't been able to come up with any negatives, aside from the uniform prior restriction which I don't find problematic so far.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why do I need a parameter for the hypermean...
parts:
For a start, it doesn't define a proper density because
the following doesn't evaluate to 1

INTEGRAL_Theta p(theta | sd) d.theta

= INTEGRAL_Theta PROD_i normal(theta[i] | mean(theta), sd) d.theta

This is easy to see because p(theta | y) = p(theta + c | y)
for any c, so there's an infinite-mass ridge as discussed in
the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.

From a more practical perspective, you also need the uncertainty
in theta to make predictions about new theta observations and you
may want to include a prior for mu.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why do I need a parameter for the hypermean...
parts:
On May 19, 2016, at 6:08 PM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok. Re-read the problematic posterior section, still struggling to see the infinite mass ridge point, if you or anyone wants to take another try it would be very welcome, otherwise maybe something sinks in over coming days... so far as I see the mass of mean(theta) will be determined by the individual theta likelihoods and sd, in much the same way as the mass of a mu sampled from a uniform distribution.

For a proper density p(theta), INTEGRAL p(theta) d.theta = 1.
You define

p(theta) = PROD_i normal(theta[i] | mean(theta), sd)

and the integral diverges to infinity. More intuitively,
the ridge is a line of constant density, so if you draw
a small circle around it, you get a cylinder of infinite mass.

- Bob

Given that

p(theta | y ) = ( p(y|theta) p(theta)  )   /  p(y)  with theta~ uniform(-5,5)

is a well behaved model, what is it about the inclusion of a hyperprior on the sd of theta...

This approach is working much more efficiently for dynamic modelling problems, recovering parameters well, and I realised priors on mean(theta) can also be included, so no restriction to uniform (according to the current, apparently invalid, logic!).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why do I need a parameter for the hypermean...
parts:
But I still don't understand why you're writing such
a non-identified model.

- Bob

> On May 23, 2016, at 10:13 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Since myself and colleagues still don't see the point, I will try to re-phase, but of course ignore if it's getting frustrating! I just wonder if there is a miscommunication.
>
> Given that
> p(theta | y ) = ( p(y|theta) p(theta) ) / p(y) with theta~ uniform(-5,5)
> is a well behaved model,

So far, you've only defined p(theta). For the model to be
well behaved, INTEGRAL p(theta | y) d.theta has to be finite.

> what is it about the inclusion of a hyperprior on the sd of theta...
> p(theta, sd | y ) = ( p(y|theta) p(theta | sd) p(sd) ) / p(y) with theta<lower=-5,upper=5> ~ normal(mean(theta),sd) and sd~uniform(0,100)
> that apparently causes the integral to diverge to infinity?

If theta is bounded to (-5,5) you'll get a normalizable
posterior.

The problem I was referring to is that this term (where theta is an N-vector
and sd > 0),

p(theta | sd) = PROD_n normal(theta[n] | mean(theta), sd),

is not normalizable in that INTEGRAL p(theta | sd) d.theta = infinity.

If you bound each theta[n] to (-5,5), the integral will be finite.

But I still don't understand what you think p(theta | sd) is saying
about theta conditional on sd. Maybe it'd help if you fix a sd,
take N=2 and make a 2D plot of theta[1] x theta[n] in (-5,5) vs. density
with a fixed sigma so you can see what the issue is.

We generally don't recommend bounding parameters because it can
cause problems both statistically (truncating and hence underestimating
uncertainty) and computationally (transforms to unconstrained space
stretch the boundaries).

Why not just make theta uniform on (-5,5)^N? Or normal centered around
0 if you want shrinkage.

- Bob
